Case study / 01

AI video.
The limits of control.

A graduate group project combining creative concept development, generative visuals and promotional storytelling.

Generative AIVisual storytellingCollaboration
Published video ↗

A tool can produce a convincing image without producing a coherent film. Working on an original retail concept made that gap tangible.

Original portfolio video still

Frame excerpt from my previously prepared portfolio, linked to the group video on LinkedIn. It is not a newly generated illustration.

The brief
Develop an original physical retail or service concept and present it as a 13–15-minute digital artefact, including a promotional advert.
My contribution
Helped coordinate the group's brand direction, created AI-assisted visuals and contributed to image-to-video work and final editing.
Where it broke down
Keeping visual elements consistent between scenes and producing the intended movement through prompts were both difficult, even when the desired effect was clear to the team.
What it demonstrated
Tool capability and task suitability are different: the output still needs to be reviewed against the creative brief, narrative coherence and audience experience.
91/100Overall group artefact mark, not an individual AI grade
13–15 minAssigned digital artefact format
Provenance / limitationsThe video link comes from an earlier portfolio PDF. Specific prompts and iteration counts are not documented, so this case does not claim a particular prompt engineering method or improved output from unverified steps.
Case study / 02

When a
search term misleads.

An independent written investigation conducted during a voluntary UK marketing internship.

Google TrendsAudience researchInsight translation
Selected project excerpts only; internal report not reproduced.

Five years of search history looked relevant until I checked what people meant by the word “Pathfinder”.

“The keyword ‘Pathfinder’ is heavily dominated by the gaming (Pathfinder 2e) and automotive (Nissan) sectors.”Extract from my original report, 23 February 2026
Question
Could broad brand-search interest reliably represent awareness among international students?
Evidence
Reviewed five years of UK Google Trends and related queries, identifying unrelated searches for a role-playing game and a vehicle.
Recommendation
Use more audience-specific terms such as “International Student Support UK” instead of interpreting generic name searches as a demand proxy.
Separate idea
Proposed a three-colour brand narrative: orange for connection, green for adaptation and blue for opportunity.
Follow-up
Co-planned Instagram content concepts with the founder; the proposal received positive internal feedback. The content was not launched during my internship.
Orange Connection
Green Adaptation
Blue Opportunity
Original document / evidence disciplineA complete text transcription of the accessible original five-page report is available above. Some early interpretations in that original report infer student demand from ambiguous search trends; they are preserved as historical thinking, not endorsed here as verified findings. The full Word layout and embedded charts are not reproduced. The separate “What Is Home?” interviews are not presented as proof of Google Trends findings.
Case study / 03

Lidl GB.
Beyond the headline.

A self-directed UK grocery-market dashboard and a customer-insight question built from public sources.

Power BIPower QueryDAXMarket insight

I built the dashboard myself and selected its questions: market share, competition, shopper switching and proposed store expansion. But national data was only the starting point.

UK grocery market · Competitive snapshot

Lidl8.6%
0%10%20%30%

Bar lengths use a shared 0–30% axis so differences match the stated market-share figures.

Lidl vs Aldi2.2 percentage-point gap
What the data does not establishA 2.2 percentage-point national gap between Aldi and Lidl does not tell us whether local accessibility, habit, price perception or loyalty activity explains an individual's store choice. Testing those drivers would require further data.
Original values: independently prepared October 2026 Lidl customer-insight note, citing Worldpanel by Numerator / DEFRA. Chart redrawn for this website from the note; it is not a screenshot of the Power BI file.
The task I set
Use public UK grocery sources to compare Lidl with major retailers and organise the story through market share, retailer gaps, switching gains and expansion plans.
Build
Prepared data with Excel / Power Query and built interactive measures and comparisons in Power BI, including DAX. I made the choices about which indicators mattered and how to present them.
Problem-solving
Worked through blank DAX measures and unexpected visual filtering during development. AI helped discuss technical possibilities, but did not choose or build the dashboard.
New question
What makes one retailer the habitual choice over another: convenience, price, store experience or loyalty? A personal shopper observation was treated as a hypothesis, not as measured evidence.
8.6%Lidl share in the cited 12-week snapshot
2.2 ppSnapshot gap to Aldi, not a five-year trend
Work sample transparencyEarlier conversations contain the Lidl `.pbit` template, dashboard preview PNG, Excel and customer-insight PDFs. Their filenames and content were located and reviewed; the original bytes were not exportable into this website session. The redrawn chart above uses confirmed figures, not invented dashboard screenshots. This was independent portfolio work, not commissioned by Lidl GB.
Case study / 04

FitFlop UK.
Two lenses,
one market.

An independently built two-page Power BI report. The actual source screen recording is available here.

Original screen capturePower BIPublic-data analysis
Download compressed demo ↗

Product-and-price structure answers a different question from branded search-interest. I kept those two views distinct.

Actual capture · Page 01

Products & sample: product category counts, average current price and family-level comparison.

Actual capture · Page 02

UK branded search interest, competitor positioning and five-year search-index context.

Real user-uploaded Power BI screen recording from 14 October 2026, transcoded for web playback. It has not been recreated from a prompt.

Page 01
Examined publicly observable FitFlop product families, product counts and price distribution. Used filter and visual interactions to inspect category differences.
Page 02
Compared five-year UK Google Trends branded search-interest indices and exploratory positioning across FitFlop, Birkenstock, Skechers, Onitsuka Tiger and Clarks.
My ownership
Built the report and chose analysis focus, dashboard story and visual priorities. Used public material, not internal sales, customer or campaign records.
Data limits
Google Trends provides relative indices, not revenue, units sold or customer counts. Public product assortments do not reveal actual company conversion or profitability.
Real primary evidenceThe two screenshots and the playable recording come from the previously uploaded original FitFlop Power BI capture (14 October 2026). The web video is a compressed copy for accessibility. No performance impact or employer adoption is claimed.
Working method

Evidence first.
Judgement always.

The same pattern appears in visual experimentation, self-directed dashboards and organisational research: an output is only useful when it is relevant to the question and can be explained.

01 / QuestionDefine what needs to be understood before selecting the tool or visual.
02 / VerifyCheck whether the data or model output actually supports the conclusion.
03 / TranslatePresent findings, limitations and possible next steps to the people using them.
About / HyunJung Kwak

Analytical by habit.
Curious by practice.

I completed taught modules in MSc Marketing at the University of Birmingham and submitted my dissertation; the degree award is pending. My work spans UK audience research, assessed mixed-method analysis, hands-on AI coursework and personally built Power BI portfolios.

In earlier professional teaching work I compared assessment results, identified recurring errors, adapted guidance across proficiency levels and followed up on progress. That experience shapes how I approach technology adoption: useful tools also need clear explanations for the people expected to use them.

What this portfolio does — and does not — claim

  • Lidl and FitFlop are independent public-data portfolios, not paid client work.
  • Search indices are not sales figures; hypothetical questions are not presented as achieved business impact.
